https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg7k.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Zolani Tete was in training for a comeback fight when he was killed By Khanyisile Ngcobo ,Â Reporting from Johannesburg Â and Â Jude Winter ,Â BBC Sport Published 4 hours ago Four people have been arrested in South Africa in connection with the murder of boxing champion Zolani Tete, who was shot dead outside his home on Friday. Tete, 38, was gunned down in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape. A young woman who was with him was also shot and is in hospital. One of the men being held, a 22-year-old who was arrested on Saturday, will make an initial appearance in court on Monday, and faces murder and attempted murder charges. Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014. He was later given a four-year ban, which lapsed in July this year. The remaining suspects, who were arrested on Sunday, are due in court on Tuesday. Two have been charged with unlawful possession of firearms and ammunition. It is unclear whether they will also be charged with murder and attempted murder. Tete was in his car waiting for the gate to his house to open when two armed suspects in balaclavas emerged from a vehicle and fired "multiple shots" at him and a 27âyearâold female passenger, according to officials. The motive behind the attack is unclear. Tributes have been pouring in for the two-time world champion since his death. South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said: "South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced." Former Sports Minister Fikile Mbalula also paid tribute to Tete, lamenting the loss of a "a great South African who has made an immense contribution in the sport of boxing". Tete beat Liverpool's Paul Butler in 2015 in one of the eight times he fought in the United Kingdom. He also holds a Guinness World Record for the fastest knockout in a title fight, ending his match with Siboniso Gonya inside 11 seconds in 2017. Tete last fought in July 2022, beating Briton Jason Cunningham by knockout In London, but it was later ruled a no-contest after he failed a drugs test. He tested positive for anabolic steroid stanozolol and was given a ban by the UK Anti-Doping Agency. After his death, manager Mla Tengimfene confirmed he had been training for a comeback fight after his ban ended. Tete had 29 wins in 34 fights, with four losses and one no-contest. South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world. According to the latest crime statistics, covering the period between January and March this year, around 58 people were killed each day. http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27929.text: Big News Network.com Kallas says Europe should not give without getting anything in return in Ukraine peace deal VILNIUS, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Europe should not give without getting anything in return in any future peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Monday, stressing that any peace settlement would also involve commitments from Europe. Kallas made the remarks during a visit to Lithuania after U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend in renewed diplomacy to end the war. At a joint press conference with Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius, Kallas was asked whether the weekend talks had brought peace closer and what a possible trilateral summit without an EU seat would mean for Europe's ability to shape the outcome. She said Russia and Ukraine ultimately needed to talk directly to each other. "On the European side, it is clear that we cannot be mediators between Russia and Ukraine. They need to talk to each other. We have always been on the side of Ukraine, so we are not neutral in this situation," Kallas said. She said that any eventual peace agreement would also involve "a lot of asks for Europe," adding that these were not things Europe should give "without getting anything in return." Earlier on Monday, Kallas met Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda and discussed Lithuania's priorities for its upcoming presidency of the Council of the European Union. Nauseda said Lithuania would focus on European security and defence, EU enlargement, competitiveness, internal security and social resilience during its presidency. Photograph: Family handout Greenland After so long in Trump’s sights, hopeful Greenlanders breathe a collective sigh of relief Locals hope agreement signed this week is step towards independence and end to US threats to annex island Miranda Bryant Nordic correspondent Thu 24 Sep 2026 10.27 EDT Last modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 10.43 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google G reenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and Múte B Egede, the foreign minister, received a hero’s welcome when they landed back in Nuuk from New York on Wednesday night – and a nation took a collective sigh of relief. Colleagues, friends and members of the public turned out to greet them at an airport where, just 20 months ago, the landing of a Trump-branded plane containing Donald Trump Jr had kickstarted a geopolitical crisis that the people of Greenland now hope is over. To cheers and applause, and waving red and white Erfalasorput flags, the politicians were credited with saving the nation thanks to a new defence agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the US signed this week at the UN in New York. It comes after an unprecedented period of turbulence in which Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to invade the Arctic island and almost tore apart Nato in the process. 1:09 Greenland leaders receive hero's welcome after signing security pact with US and Denmark – video “Welcome home,” the speaker of Inatsisartut, the Greenlandic parliament, Kim Kielsen, said. “Welcome to a country that we were about to lose. You have ensured that we have a future here.” Like many Greenlanders, for the last year-and-a-half he said he had been holding his breath. Nielsen, who became prime minister last year in the middle of the crisis, told the crowd: “We can be calm. Our land will not be taken. Our land will not be bought. The road has been long, and it has been very difficult and dangerous.” Hundreds then attended a celebratory coffee party at Katuaq, the Greenlandic capital’s cultural centre. Aqqalukkuluk Fontain, 38, who was there with his girlfriend, Stella, and their youngest daughter, Aura, who is three, said the collective release of tension was palpable. “It was a joyous moment. It’s going to linger for a while,” said the IT manager, who earlier this year organised a protest outside the new US embassy in Nuuk. He cautioned he could not entirely relax – concerned that, after the midterms, Trump could change his mind and relations could “take a turn for the worse” – but hailed the deal with the US as a moment of pride for Greenland and a stroke of “strategy genius” from Greenlandic and Danish negotiators. “Trump is trying to angle it that he made a great deal. But he wanted total control, ownership of Greenland. He didn’t get that,” he said. View image in fullscreen Donald Trump, Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister of Denmark; and Jens-Frederik Nielsen, the prime minister of Greenland, at the UN headquarters this week. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Its full text contains some key differences from the 1951 defence agreement it is intended to update – for example, the US gets underwater access to Greenland and specific permission to construct a missile defence system – but is a far cry from Donald Trump’s original threat to annex the Arctic island. And in terms of tangible outcomes, the biggest winner is arguably Greenland, where it is seen as a potential stepping stone to future independence. When the 1951 agreement was signed, Greenland was still a colony of Denmark . Now, it is a largely autonomous territory that has signed an agreement alongside Denmark with the US that it played a central role in negotiating. A big question hanging over Greenland independence was what would happen to its status within Nato and relationship with the US. The new agreement answers that question. It stipulates that if it did become independent, the governments of Greenland and Denmark would “together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will agree to remain in Nato, including by applying to become a member if necessary”. View image in fullscreen Trump, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio; Lars Løkke Rasmussen, the Danish foreign minister; Frederiksen, Nielsen and Egede. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images The centrality of Nato to the agreement is also seen as a boost for an alliance that was creaking under US claims against one of its fellow members’ territory. Greenlandic politician Qarsoq Høegh-Dam, who earlier this year became the first member of the pro-independence party Naleraq to be elected to the Danish parliament, said there was still considerable work to do in terms of gaining independence but that “a lot of what ifs” have now gone. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Denmark reportedly flew blood bags to Greenland in preparation for a US attack Read more “It’s a point of relief for Greenlanders,” he said. “They can lower their shoulders a bit, so we can talk about domestic issues, the road to independence more freely, instead of the search of what if?” Much of the agreement already existed in practice, he said, but now “it is written in ink” with Greenland’s explicit involvement. “It’s a continuation of an agreement since the 1950s. The difference is now that Greenland has some say in it. They want to agree for themselves instead of a country overseas agreeing on behalf of them,” he said. “That’s the difference first and foremost and it is significant.” View image in fullscreen People protesting against Trump’s policy towards Greenland at the US consulate in Nuuk, Greenland, in January. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP He said, however, there were still questions about what the words will equate to in practice, for example on investment. “It’s a good foundation, but the details are missing,” he said. View image in fullscreen Aviaja Fontain: ‘We don’t have to think about getting attacked and just live our peaceful life again.’ Photograph: Inesa Matuliauskaite/The Guardian Given that just a few months ago Trump was threatening to invade Greenland, and a few weeks since he posted a map of Greenland covered with the US flag to social media, in many ways the very fact that a diplomatic agreement has been reached is a victory in itself. Ulrik Pram Gad, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS), said: “For Danes and Greenlanders, it’s a win to be able to force Trump into doing something diplomatically. And if this actually puts the Greenland crisis to rest, it will be felt as a win for Greenland, Denmark and Europe because then we can concentrate on real problems and trying to find ways to work with the US on that.” Aviaja Fontain, 41, a student from Nuuk, said the agreement puts to rest months of anxiety. At one point, amid government warnings about preparedness, she thought Nuuk was being attacked by the US during what turned out to be a power cut caused by a storm. “Many of us have been afraid that Trump will use force, but now I can feel relief,” she said. Now she feels she can finally relax. “We don’t have to think about getting attacked and just live our peaceful life again.” Explore more on these topics Greenland Trump administration Denmark US foreign policy Europe Donald Trump Nato features Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Greenland forces Trump-linked US oil firm to delay drilling Trump renews call for US to take over Greenland as he arrives for Nato summit Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen to lead four-party coalition after months of uncertainty Greenlanders are not ‘experimental subjects’, says minister as she decries US doctor’s visit Denmark reportedly flew blood bags to Greenland in preparation for a US attack Canada and France open Greenland consulates in show of Denmark support Trump’s Greenland threats open old wounds for Inuit across Arctic Greenland threats no laughing matter, says mayor after comic’s flag stunt Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
